DECISION AND ORDER
A formal hearing on the above-referenced protest was held on December 6, 2011, before
Sally Galanter, Hearing Officer. The Taxation and Revenue Department (“Department”) was
represented by Mr. Nelson Goodin, Chief Legal Counsel for the Department. California Closets
was represented by its President, Mr. Ronald. R. Young (“Taxpayer”). In addition to the
documents contained in the administrative file articulated at the beginning of the hearing to
include Taxpayer’s submission of documents dated November 3, 2011, the following document
is admitted into the record: Department Exhibit A. Based on the evidence and arguments
presented, IT IS DECIDED AND ORDERED AS FOLLOWS:

4. Taxpayer had paid gross receipts and withholding tax in full for each period prior
to the assessments being issued.
5. Gross Receipts and Withholding taxes are reported and paid under New Mexico’s
Combined Reporting System (“CRS system”). Taxes reported under the CRS system are due on
the twenty-fifth day of the month following the month in which the taxable event occurs.
Because Taxpayer was a monthly filer under the CRS system, gross receipts and withholding
taxes would be due and owing on the twenty-fifth day of the month following the month in
In the matter of the protest of California Closets
Page 2

which taxes were collected.
6. Some of the payments were no more than a day or two late and some of the
payments were a month or two late.
7. On February 1, 2011, Taxpayer filed a formal written protest to each assessment.
The protests were received by the Department’s Protest office on February 8, 2011 and accepted
as timely by Department letter dated February 16, 2011.
8. Taxpayer received notification from the Department of a substantial overpayment
shortly after filing each return, with instructions for claiming the overpayment or amending its
tax return.
9. Taxpayer did not apply for a refund for each received Notice of Overpayment as
Taxpayer had determined that taxes had been properly paid for each tax period.
10. Each time Taxpayer received Department notification of an overpayment,
Taxpayer contacted the Department at the telephone number indicated in the Notice of
Overpayment and was told to ignore the letter of overpayment.
11. Unsatisfied with the Department’s response to the Notices of Overpayments, upon
receipt of the July 31, 2010, Notice of Overpayment, Taxpayer applied for refund. Taxpayer
thereafter received notification from the Department that it had received the claim for refund and
that the refund was being denied as no overpayment existed.
12. Mr. Tom Dillon is a Protest Auditor for the Department. Mr. Dillon audited
Taxpayer’s file and prepared an accounting of the outstanding interest and penalty due the
Department based on when the tax was due and when it was paid for each tax period.
In the matter of the protest of California Closets
Page 3

[Department Exhibit A]
13. For each of the tax periods covered by the assessments, the payments were
received by the Departments after the twenty-fifth of the month following the month in which
the taxes were collected.
14. Mr. Dillon testified that the Department looks to the postmark date of the return,
if it is available, to determine if the return is timely submitted. If a postmark is not available, then
the Department notes the day the documentation and payment are received.
15. Taxpayer attempted to timely submit all taxes due however Taxpayer had no
documentation as to when the payments were made or when they were mailed to the Department.
DISCUSSION
The issue to be determined is whether Taxpayer is liable for interest and civil penalty
assessed due to late filing of its CRS returns for gross receipts and withholding tax. Taxpayer,
each time, paid the full principal payment, according to the Department, but did not file the
returns timely. The Department assessed Taxpayer interest and penalty for each late filing.
Taxpayer claimed that interest and penalty should be abated on each assessment as the letters
received from the Department, as to the overpayments, led Taxpayer to believe that each
payment had been received, properly processed and the returns were complete and proper.
Taxpayer also claimed that the conversations with Department employees misled Taxpayer into
thinking that the returns were complete and proper. Additionally, Taxpayer claimed that the
Department delayed in notifying Taxpayer of the late filings for eighteen months Taxpayer
claimed that had the Department notified Taxpayer immediately as to the first late payment,
In the matter of the protest of California Closets
Page 4

Taxpayer would have corrected the error and made sure that all subsequent payments were
timely made. Taxpayer asserted that the Department’s failure to timely notify Taxpayer led to
substantial additional assessments.
Burden of Proof.
NMSA 1978, §7-1-17 (C) (2007), states that any assessment of taxes made by the
Department is presumed to be correct. Holt v. New Mexico Department of Taxation & Revenue,
2002-NMSC-34, ¶4, 133 N.M. 11, 59 P.3d 491. NMSA 1978, §7-1-3 (2009), defines tax to
include not only the amount of tax principal imposed but also, “unless the context otherwise
requires, the amount of any interest or civil penalty relating thereto.” See also El Centro Villa
Nursing Center v. Taxation and Revenue Department, 108 N.M. 795, 779 P. 2d 982 (Ct. App.
1989). Accordingly, it is Taxpayer’s burden to come forward with evidence and legal documents
to establish that he is entitled to an abatement of the assessment, in full or in part.
Date Tax Returns Due.
NMSA 1978, §7-9-11 (1969) requires that gross receipts taxes are to be paid on or before
the twenty-fifth day of the month following the month in which the taxable event occurs.
[emphasis added]. NMSA 1978, §7-3-6 (2010) requires that taxes withheld under the provisions
of the Withholding Tax Act [7-3-1 NMSA 1978] must be paid on or before the twenty-fifth day
of the month following the month when the taxes were required to be withheld. [emphasis
added]. Taxpayer is a monthly filer under the CRS system. Therefore each monthly payment was
required to be timely postmarked or received by the Department on or before the twenty-fifth
day of the month following the collection of the tax.
In the matter of the protest of California Closets
Page 5

Regulation 3.2.2.9 NMAC (04/30/2001) explains that the timeliness of a return is
governed by NMSA 1978, Section 7-1-9 of the Tax Administration Act and its regulations.
NMSA 1978, §7-1-9 (B) (1997) requires that payments by mail are timely “if mailed on or
before the date on which they are required.” NMSA 1978, §7-1-13 (B) (2007) requires each
taxpayer to complete and file tax returns “on or before the date on which payment of any tax is
due.” NMSA 1978, §7-1-13 (B) (2007) and Regulation 3.1.4.10 (C) (1) NMAC (06/30/2010)
allow for the determination of timeliness based on the postmark on the envelope used to submit
the return. The regulation explains that if the postmark does not bear a date on or before the date
prescribed for timely mailing, the “payment will be presumed to be late.” The regulations places
the burden on the sender to ensure timely mailing and receipt by the Department stating,
Accordingly, the sender who relies upon the applicability of Section 7-1-9 NMSA
1978 assumes the responsibility that the postmark will bear a date on or before
the last date prescribed for filing…or for making the payment.
Taxpayer was unable to establish that the payments were made by the date prescribed by law.
The Department’s records reflect payments were received late for each of the CRS returns.
Timeliness of Assessment.
Taxpayer questioned why the Department took so long to notify it of the late filings. Mr.
Young testified that had he been notified immediately he would have corrected the problem
immediately. Instead, eighteen months elapsed prior to being notified that the CRS returns were
not being filed timely. Rather than one assessment for late filing, Taxpayer received ten
assessments for late filing substantially increasing the accumulated interest and penalty. The
Department offered no explanation as to the delay in issuing the assessments or to the numerous
In the matter of the protest of California Closets
Page 6

documents sent to Taxpayer as to overpayments on each filed return. Acknowledging Taxpayer’s
legitimate confusion, due to the oral and written communications with the Department, Taxpayer
is mistaken in its perception that the Department had a duty to notify Taxpayer when payments
were not timely made and that when the Department did not do so, it was not acting in good
faith.
It certainly would be beneficial for a taxpayer if the Department were to notify each
taxpayer when a mistake in made in a filing and/or in a payment. However, the Department
certainly does not have the personnel to individually review and audit each taxpayer’s return to
search for errors and then notify each taxpayer as to the results of the review and audit. Neither
does the Department have the legal obligation to assume the taxpayer’s responsibility pursuant to
New Mexico law. The New Mexico tax system includes a self-reporting tax requirement.
According to NMSA 1978, §7-1-13(B) (2007), it is the obligation of each taxpayer, not the
Department, to accurately determine his/her tax liability and report those liabilities to the state in
a timely manner. See Tiffany Construction Co. V. Bureau of Revenue, 90 N.M. 16, 17, 558 P.2d
1155, 1156 (Ct. App. 1976), cert denied, 90 N.M. 255, 561 P. 2d 1348 (1977). Taxpayer, not the
Department, had the responsibility to know the date for filing of the CRS returns and to timely
file the returns.
Pursuant to NMSA 1978, §7-1-18 (A) (1994), the Department is allowed three years from
the end of the calendar year in which the tax is due to issue an assessment. The assessments were
issued within the time period allowed by law. The evidence established that Taxpayer was trying
to fulfill its tax obligations and timely pay the full taxes owed. The evidence established that
In the matter of the protest of California Closets
Page 7

Taxpayer was receiving mixed communications from the Department. Taxpayer had no evidence
as to when the returns were actually mailed to the Department. Taxpayer did file CRS returns for
each month. The Department’s records reveal that each of the returns covered by the assessments
were filed after the date for timely filing. Taxpayer had the duty to overcome the presumption of
correctness by establishing that the payments were made timely. Taxpayer was unable to sustain
it burden of proof and prove when the payments were actually mailed or received by the
Department. The evidence established that the CRS returns were not filed timely. Therefore the
assessments were issued by the Department based on the late filings.
Estoppel.
The evidence established that Taxpayer was assessed penalty and interest for late filing of
its CRS returns. Taxpayer argued that the Department should be stopped from enforcing
collection of the penalty and interest based on both the verbal and written communications
received from the Department employees. The adjudicative functions of an administrative
agency like the Department are considered by New Mexico courts to be “quasi-judicial” powers.
According to the New Mexico Supreme Court, the quasi-judicial powers of an administrative
agency do not include the authority to grant equitable relief to a party before the agency,
although a court may later do so after the administrative action is completed. [emphasis added].
See AA Oilfield Service v. New Mexico State Corporation Commission, 118 N.M. 273, 279, 881
P.2d 18, 24 (1994).
Even if the Department’s administrative Hearing Officers had the authority to grant
equitable relief, principals of equitable estoppel generally do not apply to the facts in this case.
In the matter of the protest of California Closets
Page 8

As a general rule, courts are reluctant to apply the doctrine of equitable estoppel against the state.
This general rule is given even greater weight in cases involving the assessment and collection of
taxes. See Kerr-McGee Nuclear Corp. v. Property Tax Division, 95 N.M. 685, 625 P.2d 1202
(Ct. App. 1980). Our courts have determined that estoppel will not be applied against a state
governmental entity “unless there is a shocking degree of aggravated and overreaching conduct
or where right and justice demand it.” Wisznia v. State, Human Servs. Dep’t, 1998-NMSC-11,
P17, 125 N.M. 140, 958 P.2d 98. In determining whether estoppel is appropriate, the conduct of
both parties must be considered Gonzales v. Public Employees Retirement Board, 114 NM 420,
427, 839 P.2d 630, 637, cert. denied, 114 Nm 227, 836 P.2d 1248 (1992).
In examining the conduct of both parties, the courts have been willing to grant estoppel
when a party has relied on written representations. Here, Taxpayer claimed that he relied on the
oral representations of employees of the Department although he was not able to recall the names
of any Department employees providing him information. The oral statements of a Department
employee do not give rise to estoppel. In Taxation and Revenue Department v. Bien Mur Indian
Market, Inc., 108 N.M. 228, 231, 770 P.2d 873, 876 (1989), the court held that the taxpayer “did
not act reasonably in relying on the oral representation of the Department.” Additionally, the
written over-payment communications from the Department did not provide any notification to
Taxpayer that the CRS returns were timely filed. The evidence did not establish that either the
Department’s written or verbal communications evidenced “affirmative misconduct on the part
of the Department.
It was a misunderstanding for Taxpayer to have interpreted the Notices of Overpayment
In the matter of the protest of California Closets
Page 9

as indicating that each payment was timely filed and without any issue. None of the Notices of
Overpayment provide any information as to the timeliness of the filing of the return. The
assessments, timely issued to Taxpayer, indicate the Department‘s determination that while the
payments were made, the payments were not timely. Based on New Mexico’s self-reporting tax
system and based on the evidence that Taxpayer did not fulfill its reporting obligations, the facts
do not support a finding of estoppel.
Interest.
NMSA 1978, §7-1-67 (2007) governs the imposition of interest on late payment of tax,
providing in pertinent part:
A. If a tax imposed is not paid on or before the day on which it becomes
due, interest shall be paid to the state on that amount from the first day
following the day on which the tax becomes due, without regard to any
extension of time or installment agreement, until it is paid… [emphasis added].
The Legislature’s use of the word “shall” indicates that the provisions of the statute are
mandatory rather than discretionary. State v. Lujan, 90 N.M. 103, 105, 560 P.2d 167, 169 (1977).
See also, NMSA 1978, §12-2A-4 (A) (1997) of the Uniform Statute and Rule Construction Act
(the words “shall” and “must” express a duty, obligation, requirement or condition precedent).
With limited exceptions that do not apply here, Section 7-1-67 directs the Department to assess
interest whenever taxes are not timely paid. Regulation 3.1.4.10 (A) NMAC (06/30/10) titled
“Filing Returns - Due Date” explains that a taxpayer is liable for interest if the tax is not paid
when due.
The assessment of interest is designed to compensate the state for the time value of
unpaid revenues. In this matter, Taxpayer correctly paid the amount of tax due however the
In the matter of the protest of California Closets
Page 10

returns were not sent to the Department to be received by the date the tax was due. As a result of
this failure Taxpayer, not the state, had the use of the principal tax due between the date when
payment was due and the date when each payment was actually received by the Department.
Therefore, while acknowledging that the error was unintentional, Taxpayer had use of the money
legally due the state, even, as revealed in some instances, if only for a few days. As the tax was
not paid within the statutorily mandated time period, interest was appropriately due and charged
until the payment was received by the Department.
Penalty.
NMSA 1978, §7-1-69 (A) (2007) provides:
in the case of failure due to negligence or disregard of department rules
and regulations, but without intent to evade or defeat a tax, … to file
by the date required a return regardless of whether a tax is due, there shall
be added to the amount assessed a penalty in an amount equal to the
greater of:…(2) two percent per month or any fraction of a month from
the date the return was required to be filed multiplied by the tax liability
established in the late return, not to exceed twenty percent of the tax liability
established in the late return;
When a taxpayer fails to file required tax returns by the date required “regardless of whether tax
is due” as a result of negligence or disregard of the rules and regulations, Section 7-1-69 (A) (2)
imposes a penalty of two percent per month or any fraction of a month “from the date the return
was required to be filed,” not to exceed twenty percent of the outstanding tax liability established
in the late return. The statute imposes a penalty based on negligence for failure to timely file a
return. Regulation 3.1.4.10 (A) NMAC (06/30/2010) requires that if a report is not filed when it is
due because of negligence of the taxpayer, the taxpayer will also be liable for penalty. The good
faith of a Taxpayer is not an issue. What is to be determined is whether Taxpayer was negligent in
In the matter of the protest of California Closets
Page 11

failing to timely file a return.
In this matter, Taxpayer had a duty to know when the CRS returns were due and to timely
file them with the Department. Taxpayer failed to timely file the CRS returns. By failing to ensure
that the CRS returns and payments were timely received by the Department, Taxpayer was
negligent and liable for the penalty assessed by the Department. This error meets the definition of
negligence set out in Department regulations and in New Mexico case law. Taxpayer failed to carry
his burden to establish that he was not negligent, that he timely submitted the CRS reports and
timely paid the gross receipts and withholding tax. Therefore Taxpayer is liable for the penalty
assessment. See El Centro Villa Nursing Center v. Taxation & Revenue Department, 108 N.M.
795, P.797, 779 P.2d 982, 984 (Ct. App. 1989) (§ 7-1-69 is designed specifically to penalize
unintentional failure to pay tax.).
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
A. Taxpayer filed a timely, written protest to the assessments issued and
Jurisdiction lies over the parties and the subject matter of this protest.
B. Taxpayer failed to meet its burden to establish timely filing of its CRS
returns.
C. By failing to timely file its CRS returns as set forth in NMSA 1978, §7-9-11
(1966), Taxpayer is liable for the interest assessed by the Department pursuant to NMSA 1978,
§7-1-67.
D. The amount of civil penalty was correctly added and assessed, pursuant to
NMSA
In the matter of the protest of California Closets
Page 12

1978, §7-1-69(A) (2).
For the foregoing reasons, Taxpayer protest is DENIED.
